You were born on a day that most years simply doesn't exist.

February 29, 1960 was a Monday — one of the rarest calendar coordinates a person can occupy. In an ordinary year, the world moves from February 28 straight into March without pausing for you. Every four years, it remembers. That peculiarity is not merely a quirk of timekeeping; it is a permanent reminder that you arrived at an extraordinary moment in an extraordinary year.

---

**The World Shook That Day**

The most dramatic event of February 29, 1960 unfolded in Morocco. Just before midnight, while most of the city slept, a shallow earthquake struck Agadir. The magnitude was modest by seismological standards, but the quake's depth was less than three kilometers — and it obliterated nearly two-thirds of the city in seconds. Roughly 12,000 to 15,000 people died. The ancient kasbah, the new city, the port neighborhoods: gone. King Mohammed V said that if the will of God was not to be questioned, the disaster in Agadir could still make a believer weep. You were born into a world that was, literally, shaking.

---

**A Leap Day Anniversary Worth Knowing**

Twenty years to the day before your birth — February 29, 1940 — Hattie McDaniel became the first African American to win an Academy Award, for her role in *Gone with the Wind*. She accepted the award in a segregated ceremony, seated at a separate table from the rest of the film's cast. Two decades later, in the weeks surrounding your birth, four Black college students in Greensboro, North Carolina had just staged a lunch counter sit-in that sparked a movement. The same struggle, two leap days apart, measured the distance between a segregated banquet table and a nation beginning — barely — to demand something better.

---

**The Year Africa Rewrote the Map**

Historians call 1960 the "Year of Africa." Seventeen nations on the continent gained independence before the year ended. The forces behind it — anti-colonial movements, European empires exhausted by two world wars, Cold War competition for newly sovereign allegiances — were already reshaping the globe when you arrived. You were born not at the end of that transformation but at its opening chapter, the moment the old map was discarded and the new one hadn't yet been drawn.

---

**Your Rarest Birthday Count**

Because February 29 reappears only in leap years, your calendar birthday has returned in 1964, 1968, and every four years since. As of today — September 8, 2026 — you have lived 66 years but turned 16 on your true birthday, most recently February 29, 2024. The next comes in 2028. You share this rarity with about one person in every 1,461 born — and with the composer Gioachino Rossini, also a February 29 arrival, who solved the social problem by observing February 28 in non-leap years.

---

**The Cold War World**

The world you entered was divided into two armed camps watching each other across a potential nuclear abyss. Eisenhower was in the White House; Khrushchev led the Soviet Union. Three years earlier, Sputnik had crossed overhead and the space race had begun. The Berlin Wall did not yet exist — it would go up in 1961 — but its psychological predecessor, the Iron Curtain, had been drawn for fifteen years. A child born in 1960 grew up in a world where the end of civilization was a genuine, daily policy consideration.

---

**Within 30 Days of Your Birth — The Sharpeville Massacre**

*Twenty-one days after you were born, on March 21, 1960, South African police opened fire on a crowd of Black protesters in the township of Sharpeville. The protesters had gathered peacefully to demonstrate against the Pass Laws requiring non-white South Africans to carry identification at all times. Sixty-nine people were killed; most were shot in the back as they fled. The massacre shocked the international community, galvanized the global anti-apartheid movement, and eventually led to South Africa's expulsion from the Commonwealth. It was the event that convinced a young Nelson Mandela that nonviolence alone could not defeat apartheid. You were three weeks old.*

---

**The World You Entered, and the World You've Seen**

A person born February 29, 1960 arrived in a world of party-line telephones, three television channels, and cars without seatbelts. In your lifetime: humans walked on the moon, the Berlin Wall fell, the Soviet Union dissolved, the internet went public, September 11 changed what security meant, a smartphone placed the sum of human knowledge in your pocket, a global pandemic stopped civilization for a year, and artificial intelligence began generating language and images at a scale no one had imagined.

You were born on a day the calendar barely acknowledges, in a year when Africa was being reborn, when the civil rights of millions were legally denied, and when the atom bomb was the most recent proof of what ingenuity could produce at its worst. The world on your 66th year would be unrecognizable to anyone present on the night of February 29, 1960.

You arrived on an extra day. The time that followed has been anything but ordinary.
